title: Four Cities, Four Stories
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Cities, like people, have different life stories. Some grow quickly and keep growing, others shrink, and a few rise and fall in a pattern that surprises even the experts who study them. To illustrate the main patterns, this passage looks at four imaginary cities, each based on a real type of place, and at the economic reasons behind the changes in their populations over a period of fifty years. Planners use such studies to decide where to build schools, roads and hospitals, and mistakes can be very expensive.

Marden began as a small market town beside a river. In the 1970s, a technology company opened its headquarters there, and other firms followed. Young graduates moved in to take the new jobs, and their children were born in the city. Since then the population has risen every single year, and it now stands at more than a million. The growth brings problems of its own, however: house prices have tripled, and many of the original residents can no longer afford to live in the neighbourhoods where they were born.

Olvia is a mining town in the mountains. For a century it prospered, but when the last coal mine closed in 1985, the main employer disappeared and families began to leave. The population has fallen steadily ever since, and several schools have been merged. The council has tried to attract tourists to the old mine buildings, but the effect so far has been small, and many of the young people who remain say that they plan to move away as soon as they finish their studies.

The history of Kessing was quite different. A car factory opened there in 1960 and the population rose rapidly, reaching a peak in 1990. Then the factory moved its production abroad, and thousands of workers lost their jobs. The population fell almost as quickly as it had risen, and it is now not much larger than it was before the factory arrived. Researchers who study such places say that cities depending on one industry are especially at risk, because a single decision in a distant boardroom can change the lives of a whole community.

Tarn followed a fourth path. It was a quiet port city whose population fell in the 1970s when the old shipping trade declined. For two decades, nothing seemed to help. Then the city turned its empty warehouses into studios, cafes and small workshops, and artists and designers began to arrive. By the early 2000s the decline had turned into recovery, and the population has now returned to about the level at which it began. Tarn is often given as an example of a city that reinvented itself.

Why do these patterns matter? According to Dr Isabel Fontaine, an urban economist, the shape of a city's population curve tells a story about its economy. Steady growth suggests a variety of jobs, a sharp rise and fall suggests dependence on a single industry, and slow decline points to a lack of opportunities for the young. She warns, though, that the pattern can change quickly, and that planners who simply extend an existing trend into the future are often proved wrong by events that nobody predicted.

What can other cities learn from these four? First, a varied economy is safer than a single large employer. Second, a city must provide homes that ordinary people can afford, or it risks losing the workers it needs. Third, empty buildings are a resource as well as a problem, as Tarn showed. Finally, planners should treat predictions with care. The future of a city, like that of its people, depends on choices that have not yet been made, and on the willingness of its citizens to adapt when the world around them changes.
